overview: “Permians” is a convenient atlas label, not the name of a documented state from 800 to 900. Scholars compare several archaeological traditions across the Upper Kama, Cheptsa, Vychegda, Vyatka, and neighboring forest zones, while historical linguistics reconstructs related Permic speech. Neither kind of evidence proves that everyone inside this polygon shared one identity, government, dialect, or daily routine. Modern Komi, Komi-Permyak, Komi-Yazva, Udmurt, and Besermyan identities have distinct histories and must not be pasted backward. The imported outline is especially misleading: it reaches the White Sea and Pechora, yet excludes Izhevsk and Sarapul, important later Udmurt places. Archaeology offers a richer picture than the color patch. Riverbank settlements, large timber houses, hearths, storage pits, fishing gear, crops, animal remains, metalworking, decorated belts, and far-traveled objects reveal communities with mixed economies and wide contacts. Burial evidence suggests social differences but cannot supply a family tree or ethnic passport. No secure local written-language sample survives from this century. A later Old Permic comparison is labeled fourteenth century, never ninth. At 900 the feature is repainted, while people, languages, households, and regional traditions continued.

periods.title: An atlas umbrella appears
periods.summary: The 800 snapshot introduces one huge feature over northern European Russia. Its geometry replaces a broader taiga category at Perm, Cherdyn, Kudymkar, Syktyvkar, Glazov, Kirov, Arkhangelsk, and Pechora. This is a cartographic classification, not evidence that a Permian state formed in 800.

periods.title: Cheptsa communities remain locally specific
periods.summary: Late Polom sites belong to the upper and middle Cheptsa basin, not to every place colored on the atlas. The final Polom phase spans the late eighth and ninth centuries. Archaeological culture names organize similar remains; they do not reveal what every inhabitant called themselves.

periods.title: Nevolino chronology reaches its close
periods.summary: The excavated Nevolino cemetery runs from the seventh century into the first quarter of the ninth. Grave goods and rites support fine chronological study and long-distance contacts. Its closing horizon cannot be turned into the disappearance, migration, or renaming of all southern Permic-speaking communities.

periods.title: Artifacts do not carry language labels
periods.summary: Researchers disagree over whether Lomovatovo remains should be called Permic, Ugric, or something else. The debate matters because pots, belts, and graves do not announce their makers’ language. Historical linguistics may support hypotheses, but an archaeological distribution is not automatically an ethnic border.

periods.title: Forest settlements support varied lives
periods.summary: Excavated sites across the Kama region show different settlement densities, chronologies, and cultural classifications. Recent source criticism warns against treating every mapped site as simultaneous or equally understood. The atlas color therefore compresses a patchwork of excavated, surveyed, poorly known, and still unknown places.

periods.title: River routes link near and far
periods.summary: Byzantine, Sasanian, Khorezmian, and Central Asian objects reached parts of the Pre-Urals by the early ninth century through exchange routes. Such finds show movement of valued things and relationships. They do not prove direct travel by every household or foreign political control over the Kama.

periods.title: Settlements organize work and defense
periods.summary: Research at major Cheptsa settlements identifies buildings, hearths, storage pits, internal divisions, expanding inhabited areas, and defensive lines. These features make planned community space visible. They do not show that every river settlement shared one layout, authority, household size, or construction history.

periods.title: Fishing steadies the food supply
periods.summary: Archaeological fish remains and tackle show that fishing supplied dependable protein and varied less by season than hunting. Rivers also shaped settlement and travel. The evidence supports skilled local fisheries, not one identical menu from the Upper Kama to the White Sea coast.

periods.title: Craft skill becomes visible
periods.summary: Ninth-century Pre-Ural jewelry begins a longer sequence of local technical traditions in casting, decoration, inlay, and gilding. Ornaments met local costume and ritual needs while styles also traveled. A beautiful buckle can reveal skilled work and contact without naming its wearer’s language.

periods.title: The label reaches a software seam
periods.summary: The 900 snapshot removes the exact feature and repaints all tested interior points as Finno-Ugric taiga hunter-gatherers. The same broad label remains at those points in 1000. Nothing in that database transition proves conquest, abandonment, or cultural regression at the century boundary.

sections.title: Read the map before reading a people into it

items.text: The exact target appears once, in the 800 border snapshot, as one polygon with one ring and 120 decoded positions. Its bounding box runs from about 36.6 to 60.3 degrees east and 56.4 to 68.8 degrees north. Those are software facts, not surveyed medieval borders.

Perm, Cherdyn, Kudymkar, Syktyvkar, Glazov, Kirov, Veliky Ustyug, Arkhangelsk, and Pechora fall inside. Izhevsk and Sarapul fall outside, as do Kazan, Ufa, Vologda, Salekhard, and Yekaterinburg. The pattern cannot stand for all later Komi or Udmurt homelands. That mismatch is historically important.

The polygon directly shares one TopoJSON arc each with Slavonic tribes, Volga Bulgars, Bashkirs, Mari, Veps, and the broad Finno-Ugric taiga feature. Shared digital arcs indicate adjacent drawing instructions. They do not establish treaties, tribute, intermarriage, warfare, language boundaries, or joint government.

At 800 every tested interior point changes from the broad Finno-Ugric taiga label to Permians. At 900 the same points change back. That symmetrical repaint looks like an atlas classification swap. It is not a hundred-year rise and fall witnessed by medieval writers.

The exact card and override are missing, while its imported summary collapses several modern peoples. Sharing the existing broad taiga card would erase this record’s one-century geometry and caveats. Sharing Volga Bulgar, Bashkir, Sami, or Slavonic cards would attach unrelated histories merely because features touch or sit nearby.

sections.title: Several archaeological regions, no single polity

items.text: Lomovatovo, Nevolino, Polom, and Vanvizdino are archaeological labels assigned to patterns in material remains. Even specialist syntheses disagree about migrations and ethnic attribution. Treat them as tools for comparing sites, dates, graves, houses, and artifacts, never as four tidy tribes with permanent borders.

Polom culture sites concentrate in the upper Cheptsa during earlier phases and expand along its middle course in later phases. The late Mydlan-Shai stage spans the late eighth through ninth centuries. This bounded basin history is more defensible than stretching one description to Arkhangelsk and Pechora.

Nevolino cemetery research dates its final stage from the last quarter of the eighth century to the first quarter of the ninth. The excavated record includes rites, objects, contact directions, and social questions. Its termination remains a cemetery chronology, not an ethnic extinction certificate.

Veryu, a Vanvizdino settlement on the middle Vychegda, is earlier than this card, dating to the sixth and seventh centuries through pottery and artifact comparison. It matters as regional background, not direct 800s evidence. Earlier layers remind us that the north already had its own sequences.

Modern linguistic categories are also diverse. Udmurt includes northern, southern, Besermyan, and central varieties, while Komi-Yazva has disputed status as language or dialect. These living classifications help expose the umbrella problem, but neither can be projected unchanged onto ninth-century archaeological sites.

sections.title: Homes, hearths, storage, and settlement planning

items.text: Eighteen excavated dwellings from Lomovatovo and later Rodanovo contexts were mainly large, timber-framed buildings with gabled construction. Hearths or furnaces and storage pits occupied the central axis. That arrangement joined warmth, cooking, work, and provisions in one carefully organized interior.

Plank floors rested on joists and could be coated with clay. Broad plank beds ran around walls, with more storage pits beneath them. The setup made the building work vertically: people rested above while supplies waited below. Medieval flat-pack furniture instructions were mercifully unnecessary.

Perimeter trenches in Lomovatovo-period houses probably supported insulating earth mounds. A house was therefore timber, soil, roof geometry, fire management, and repeated repair, not just four walls. Archaeology reveals the structure but usually loses voices, smells, bedding, and who claimed the warmest spot.

Upper Kama paleogeography identifies about twenty-five medieval sites along riverbanks between Bondyug and the Vishera mouth. Floodplains changed through time, so water access and safe building ground had to be balanced. A modern shoreline cannot simply be copied backward onto every settlement map.

Idnakar began in the ninth century and grew by expanding inhabited areas and adding defensive lines. Its Cheptsa setting shows settlement planning becoming more elaborate at one important place. It should not be promoted into the capital of every community inside the atlas polygon.

sections.title: Food from fields, forests, rivers, and herds

items.text: Pollen and plant remains from medieval Perm sites show cultivated land and mixed farming, although the best sampled settlements extend beyond this exact century. Barley, emmer, bread wheat, smaller amounts of rye and oats, and hemp appear. This supports regional possibilities, not a universal ninth-century grocery list.

Raspberry, bird cherry, and hops survived in plant samples, rare direct traces of gathering. Archaeologists note that baskets and many gathered foods usually decay, making collection harder to see than metalwork. Forest food mattered even when it did not leave a dramatic museum object.

Fish supplied relatively stable protein because fishing was less seasonal than hunting. Archaeological gear includes hooks and evidence for nets, barriers, traps, and weirs. A successful meal could depend on hydrology, patience, maintenance, and knowing fish behavior rather than heroic spear waving.

Bioarchaeological, dental, skeletal, and isotopic research finds long-term adaptation to the continental taiga environment. Such evidence can illuminate diet and workload across centuries. It cannot identify an individual’s favorite food, recipe, language, clan, social status, or whether they complained about breakfast.

Pollen from Rozhdestvenskoye records cropland and disturbance plants appearing as dark coniferous and linden forest changed around settlement. The site is later than much of this card, so it supplies a regional trajectory rather than a direct 850 snapshot. Farming altered local vegetation over time.

sections.title: Making, wearing, exchanging, and repairing things

items.text: Bayanovo’s ninth-century graves contain small bottle-shaped ornaments, many made locally and one probably imported. Their placement suggests parts of women’s belt or braid sets and perhaps needlecase amulets. A practical sewing container could also protect symbolically, giving pockets serious competition centuries early.

Perm metalwork includes buckles, beads, plaques, pendants, knife fittings, ritual plates, and animal imagery. The Hermitage dates the strongest flourishing earlier but follows the tradition into the second millennium. The pieces show long artistic memory, not a single official Permian religion or uniform costume.

Objects from Byzantium, Sasanian Iran, Khorezm, and Central Asia reached Bartym and the wider Pre-Urals by the early ninth century. Their route likely crossed Central Asia and Bashkiria before moving north. Exchange could move an object farther than its first owner ever traveled.

Later excavated workshops reveal casting, forging, bone carving, tanning, and woodworking sharing an organized production setting with hearths and chimneys. This evidence is not all ninth-century, but it helps archaeologists identify craft traces. Skill required heat control, material judgment, tools, practice, and cooperation.

Eastern silver, coins, ornaments, and costume fittings entered the Cis-Urals over many centuries, often connected to fur exchange. Some were deposited in sanctuaries or family wealth. Silver’s presence therefore may signal trade, ritual, status, storage, or reuse, not simple cash shopping.

sections.title: Families, social differences, and shared obligations

items.text: Large houses could hold several people and many tasks, but walls alone do not disclose whether residents formed a nuclear family, extended household, work group, or changing combination. Hearths, beds, and storage show shared space. Kinship labels require evidence the floor plan cannot provide.

Statistical comparison of Nevolino burials identifies social strata and changing polarization in grave treatment. Burial inequality can suggest status differences, yet grave goods express ritual choices as well as life. They are not a perfect inventory of wealth, occupation, affection, or authority.

Bayanovo ornaments appear in women’s burial contexts as belt or braid equipment. This makes women’s skilled dress and object use archaeologically visible, but a cemetery cannot provide a full division of labor. Women also worked, taught, traveled, cared, traded, and made decisions in ways graves preserve unevenly.

Everyday objects could carry protective or ritual meaning alongside practical use. Archaeologists describe a world where household and production tools might also function as amulets. That interpretation warns against splitting work and belief too neatly, while avoiding the claim that every person understood every symbol identically.

Prestigious belts and imported metalwork indicate long use, selective burial, and unequal access. One Bayanovo belt was made in the eighth century but placed in a tenth-century elite grave. Objects could outlive owners, cross generations, and gather stories that chemical analysis cannot recover.

sections.title: Children, learning, language, and a later script sample

items.text: No schoolroom, textbook, or named teacher is securely documented for this polygon in 800 to 900. Children still had to learn speech, fire safety, food processing, tool care, routes, animals, manners, and stories. Complex households and crafts make teaching necessary, but not its exact schedule or age rules.

Children are present in cemetery populations, yet grave survival and excavation practices distort age profiles. Adult-sized tools or ornaments cannot be assigned automatically to childhood lessons. The honest reconstruction is learning through participation and guidance as a likelihood, while specific games, chores, punishments, and apprenticeships remain unknown.

Craft expertise in casting, forging, sewing, hide work, pottery, fishing tackle, and building had to be transmitted. Archaeology exposes finished objects, waste, tools, and workspaces more readily than explanation or encouragement. Someone taught beginners, but the evidence rarely preserves whether that person was a parent, elder, specialist, or peer.

No securely dated local Permic writing survives from 800 to 900. Language lived in speech, names, memory, instruction, negotiation, humor, and ritual without leaving an alphabetic sample. Absence of writing is not absence of knowledge, and reconstructed language history is not a transcript of a ninth-century conversation.

Later comparison only: 𐍐 𐍑 𐍒 are Unicode Old Permic letters An, Bur, and Gai. Unicode dates the script to the fourteenth century for Komi and Komi-Permyak. These signs are at least four centuries too late and do not represent every community under the atlas label.

sections.title: Health, care, food security, and evidence limits

items.text: Skeletal, dental, and isotopic studies reveal nutrition and bodily adaptation, not a complete medical system. They can show patterns of diet, stress, disease, and activity across groups. They usually cannot tell which remedy was attempted, who provided care, what symptoms felt like, or why recovery occurred.

Buildings, hearths, storage pits, and defended settlement space affected warmth, food security, and daily risk before any special remedy was needed. Archaeology does not reveal ventilation, smoke exposure, nursing routines, or medical reasoning clearly. Daily care and uncertainty occupied the same lived environment.

Reliable fish, gathered plants, crops, animal foods, and stored provisions spread nutritional risk across seasons. The exact balance differed by site and year. Archaeologists can identify remains and isotopes, but famine memories, breastfeeding choices, illness diets, and household sharing rules are far harder to recover.

Much later Komi ethnography records massage, injury care, midwifery, herbs, fungi, and animal or plant preparations. It also documents change through migration, Russian contact, and official medicine. These records must not be projected backward as ninth-century prescriptions; they show why medical knowledge has chronology and locality.

No exact-period source reviewed here securely identifies a healer, surgical kit, medicinal recipe, hospital, or public health authority for the polygon. Saying “unknown” protects children from a made-up answer. Care certainly occurred, but its specialists, remedies, effectiveness, and spiritual dimensions cannot be filled from atlas color.

sections.title: Water, waste, cleanliness, and the toilet question

items.text: Many known settlements occupied river valleys and banks, placing travel, fish, and water nearby. Rivers also flood, shift channels, freeze, and carry waste. Paleogeography is essential because a present bank may not match a medieval one. Water access was practical knowledge, not a permanent blue line.

Hearths, storage pits, utility spaces, and work areas show that households organized clean and dirty tasks, heat, food, and materials. Excavation summaries do not preserve a sanitation manual. Sweeping, ash removal, water carrying, and vessel washing are plausible chores but lack secure ninth-century instructions.

Geophysical work at Uchkakar distinguishes dwellings, utility structures, and household or production pits, but does not identify those pits as toilets. Calling every mysterious hole a latrine would be memorable and wrong. Function requires contents, shape, location, chemistry, and context, not wishful labeling.

No reviewed exact-period source securely documents a universal Permian toilet. People still needed privacy and waste separation, but practices may have differed between farmsteads, forts, seasonal work places, and river settlements. The honest answer is evidence absent, not “everyone went in the woods.”

Food stores, fodder, livestock, dense building, fire, and site layout raised practical questions about moisture, pests, spoilage, and clutter. These are sanitation-adjacent concerns, not proof of germ theory. Protecting supplies required experience, space, and repeated chores, even without a microscope supervising the household.

sections.title: Achievements, contacts, continuity, and the false ending

items.text: Building large timber houses with framed roofs, central heating, plank floors, storage beneath wall beds, and earth insulation was a substantial engineering achievement. It coordinated woodland materials, labor, geometry, fire, and seasonal maintenance. The result deserves attention even though no palace wall survived above ground.

Local metalworkers created recognizable jewelry traditions while communities also valued distant objects. Makers controlled alloys, heat, molds, surfaces, attachments, and decoration. Exchange did not erase local invention. An imported fitting and a locally cast pendant could share one costume and tell different travel stories.

Fishing systems, cultivated plots, gathered foods, livestock, hunting, storage, and fur exchange formed mixed economies. Their strength was combination rather than one headline resource. A bad hunting season did not automatically cancel the river, field, workshop, or social relationships that helped households respond.

The atlas removes Permians in 900 and restores a broad Finno-Ugric taiga label across all tested interior points. Archaeology instead follows regional transitions into later cultures and communities at different times. One software seam cannot be treated as a conquest, disappearance, or step backward.

Komi, Komi-Permyak, Komi-Yazva, Udmurt, Besermyan, and other living communities are not interchangeable descendants of a colored polygon. Continuity includes branching, contact, migration, changing names, new institutions, and survival under pressure. Respect begins by letting each people narrate its own later history.

ending.text: The Permians feature ends at the 900 atlas seam, but the evidence does not record a single fall. Every tested interior point is simply repainted as Finno-Ugric taiga hunter-gatherers, and that broad owner remains at those points in 1000. Regional archaeological histories continued on different schedules. Polom’s late phase belongs to the ninth century; Nevolino’s excavated cemetery closes earlier within it; Lomovatovo sequences continue beyond it; and later Cheptsa, Rodanovo, and Vym developments cannot be squeezed into one instant. Families still built, fished, cultivated, gathered, stored food, worked metal, exchanged goods, buried their dead, spoke, taught children, and cared for one another. Languages and identities also changed through contact, movement, and political pressure. Modern Komi, Komi-Permyak, Komi-Yazva, Udmurt, and Besermyan histories must be followed through their own evidence, not assigned as automatic successors to this outline. The card therefore records continuity, no fall date, and no successor state.
